p-section.p-paragraph: A cheat changes a game while you play — infinite lives, a different weapon, walk through walls, and so on. RetroGo applies cheats through the running core, so whether a code works depends entirely on that core: the same code may work in one core and do nothing in another.
Every cheat is exactly one of three types. Pick the type first; the fields below it change to match.

p-list.p-item: Numeric — an address:value code such as 05C6:02. Handed to the core as a string.
Secret — an encrypted letter code such as SXNNUXSE (Game Genie / Pro Action Replay / GameShark). Also handed to the core.
Memory — a structured address + value with write mode and size. Applied by RetroArch writing memory itself.

p-section.p-paragraph: Numeric and Secret both run through the core (they only differ in the format you type). Memory is RetroArch's own memory writer.
A label for your own reference (for example Infinite Lives). It does not affect behavior. If you leave it blank, the code is used as the name.

A code in the form ADDRESS:VALUE in hexadecimal. For example 05C6:02 means “write 0x02 to memory address 0x05C6”. The core parses and applies it. This is the most common format you find online for systems like the NES.
Several sub-codes can be joined with + into one cheat, e.g. 7F80CA63+7F80CC63. The core splits them.
These are encrypted letter-and-number codes, e.g. SXNNUXSE+SZEXLEVK. They are not stored in the ROM — cheat hunters derived them, and the core decodes them.

How it works. Game Genie was originally a hardware device that sat between the cartridge and the console. It watches the CPU read the game’s program and substitutes values on the fly. A code encodes “at this ROM address, return this value” — optionally only when the address currently holds a given compare value.

The encoding. The NES Game Genie uses a 16-letter alphabet — A E P O Z X L U G K I S T V Y N — where each letter stands for 4 bits (one hex digit). A 6-letter code packs a 15-bit ROM address plus an 8-bit replacement value. An 8-letter code adds an 8-bit compare value, so the swap happens only when that address already holds the compare value (this avoids hitting the wrong location). The bits are deliberately scrambled across the letters, which is why the codes look random.
The + sign joins two or more codes into one cheat; each one patches a separate location (both are needed for the full effect).
Difference from Numeric / Memory: those write RAM every frame; a Game Genie code patches the game’s program (ROM) — for example replacing the very instruction that subtracts a life.
RetroArch writes the emulated memory itself, every frame. Use it when you want finer control (write mode, size, conditions) or prefer filling in fields instead of pasting a code.

p-list.p-item: Address — the memory address to affect, in hex (e.g. 0x05C6).
Value — the value to write, in hex (e.g. 0x02).
Write Mode — how the value is applied (see below).
Memory Size — how many bits the value occupies (see below).
Set to Value — write the value every frame, i.e. freeze it. The usual choice for “infinite” cheats.
Increase / Decrease — add or subtract the value each frame.
If Equal / Not Equal / Less Than / Greater Than (advanced) — a condition: run the next cheat in the list only when the address meets it. Used for chained, multi-line cheats.

p-section.p-paragraph: How wide the value is: 1 byte (8-bit), 2 byte (16-bit), or 4 byte (32-bit). The advanced menu adds sub-byte sizes (1 / 2 / 4 bit). Most NES cheats use 1 byte.

p-list.p-item: Big Endian — byte order for multi-byte values. The NES is little-endian; leave this off unless a platform needs it.
Address Mask — a bit mask within the byte, used only with the sub-byte (bit) sizes.

Repeat Count / Value Step / Address Step — apply the cheat to several consecutive locations: it repeats Repeat Count times, adding Value Step to the value and Address Step to the address each time (handy for things like filling every inventory slot).

p-section.p-paragraph: Numeric and Memory are the same address + value in two forms, so switching between those two types carries the data across automatically. Secret codes cannot be decoded back into an address, so they never link — keep Game Genie / PAR codes in the Secret type.

Enabling cheats may disable achievement hardcore mode. And again: whether any specific code works is up to the core — if a code does nothing, it is most likely not supported by the core you are running.
